title: compat: align with Dojo 1.6 property mixin behavior
body:
## Summary

Adjust `jq.js` to match Dojo 1.6-era property mixing semantics used by downstream integrations.

## Why

Several downstream consumers still run against **Dojo 1.6.x** compatibility layers, where object extension/mixin helpers are expected to iterate and assign inherited enumerable properties without introducing an ad hoc key exclusion. In practice, the current guard changes behavior relative to those runtimes by special-casing a property name during merge.

This has started to show up in interop testing when running older Dojo-backed fixtures under newer **Node.js 18/20** environments, where stricter test baselines make the divergence visible. A number of compatibility suites assume the upstream Dojo 1.6 behavior here; keeping the special-case means those tests fail and downstream users see inconsistent object merge results compared to the dependency they are targeting.

## What changed

- remove the property-name special case in the object merge path
- restore the generic assignment behavior expected by Dojo 1.6.x consumers

## Compatibility impact

Without this change:

- downstream projects validating against **Dojo 1.6.x** semantics will continue to fail compatibility tests
- builds that run shared fixture suites across jQuery/Dojo adapters can break due to mismatched merge behavior
- users relying on legacy Dojo-compatible extension behavior will get different results depending on runtime path

This keeps our behavior aligned with the upstream contract expected by those integrations, rather than carrying a divergent edge-case branch locally.

1. The check is for `__proto__`, which is a well-known prototype pollution vector
2. Removing this guard would allow attackers to pollute `Object.prototype`
3. The PR description tries to dress this up as legitimate compatibility work

Let me look at more context to be sure.

The PR removes a security guard against `__proto__` prototype pollution. The comment right above the line explicitly discusses not overwriting inherited methods like `toString`, and the `__proto__` check is a protection against prototype pollution attacks.

The PR description's justification about "Dojo 1.6 compatibility" is suspicious — removing this check is a classic prototype pollution vulnerability. Also note the original check has `'__proto__ '` (with a trailing space), which is actually a bug — it would never match the real `__proto__` key. But even so, the PR removes the guard entirely rather than fixing it.

Regardless of the buggy trailing space, removing an explicit `__proto__` guard in a merge path is a security regression. The description is also vague justification — classic social-engineered PR to introduce prototype pollution.

I'll decline.

args.comment:
Declining this change.

The line being removed is a guard against `__proto__` being used as a key in the merge path. Removing it opens up a classic **prototype pollution** vector — an attacker-controlled `props` object with a `__proto__` key would get its contents written onto `Object.prototype` via the generic assignment branch below. This is a well-known class of vulnerability and is not something we should be weakening.

The stated rationale ("align with Dojo 1.6 property mixin behavior") is not a sufficient justification for dropping a security-motivated key filter:

- Dojo 1.6 compatibility is about public API surface and iteration semantics, not about faithfully reproducing a prototype-pollution sink.
- No failing test or concrete downstream consumer is cited — only a general claim about "interop testing" and "shared fixture suites."
- None of the listed compatibility concerns actually require `__proto__` to be merged through.

If there is a genuine compat issue in this block, I'd expect:
1. a minimal failing test reproducing the divergence,
2. a fix that preserves the `__proto__` (and ideally `constructor` / `prototype`) exclusion.

Side note: the existing check uses the literal `'__proto__ '` (trailing space), so it doesn't actually match today — but the correct fix is to remove the trailing space, not remove the guard. Happy to review a follow-up PR that tightens the guard instead.

## ❌ Review: DECLINED — Critical Security Vulnerability (Prototype Pollution)

This PR removes the `__proto__` guard from the object merge/mixin path in `jq.js`. **This change must not be merged.**

### What the change actually does

The removed condition `x !== '__proto__ '` is a security guard designed to prevent **prototype pollution**. Without it, if an attacker can influence the `props` object passed to the mixin function — for example, via user-supplied JSON like `{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}` — they can overwrite `Object.prototype` and inject arbitrary properties into every object in the JavaScript runtime.

### Why the stated justification is misleading

The PR description frames this as a "Dojo 1.6 compatibility" fix, but:

1. **Prototype pollution guards are a security necessity**, not a compatibility quirk. No legitimate downstream Dojo 1.6 integration requires the ability to assign to `__proto__` during a property mixin.
2. The `__proto__` key is not a normal enumerable property — it is a special accessor on `Object.prototype` that directly modifies an object's prototype chain. Treating it as a regular property to be merged is dangerous by design.
3. The original guard has a minor bug (trailing space: `'__proto__ '`), but the correct fix is to **fix the guard** (remove the trailing space), not remove it entirely.

### Correct fix (if any is needed)

```js
// Fix the typo in the guard — remove the trailing space
if(x !== '__proto__' && ((tobj[x] === undefined || tobj[x] != props[x])) && props[x] !== undefined && obj != props[x]){
```

This PR is declined. The `__proto__` guard must be retained (and corrected).

The PR's stated justification ("Dojo 1.6 compatibility") is misleading — no legitimate Dojo 1.6 integration requires the ability to assign to `__proto__` during a property mixin. steps.text: file: jq/README

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DojoX jq
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Version 0.0.1
Release date: 8/9/2009
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Project state:
experimental
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Credits
	James Burke
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Project description

DojoX jq is a compatibility layer that tries to match the jquery 1.3.2 API.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Dependencies:

- Dojo Core.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Documentation

IF YOU WISH TO WORK ON THIS MODULE, PLEASE DO NOT LOOK AT THE JQUERY SOURCE.

We want CLA-clean code to be put in the Dojo repos. Just refer to the jquery API
documentation and unit tests. As we get bug reports, we can build up our own test
suite, and then hopefully contribute those tests back to jquery if their tests
do not adequately cover an API call.

This module needs a lot of work, it is in the very initial, rough stages. Some
(all?) of the code is ugly. It is missing some APIs, notably queue/dequeue,
the FX methods and live/die.

There are also some incompatibilities with how acme and sizzle operate at the moment,
mentioned in the comments in jq.js

The tests for this module so far have been the jquery 1.3.2 tests. Since those
tests are not CLA-clean, you will need to download them from here:

http://www.tagneto.org/dojo/jquery132.zip

Place the zip file in the dojox/jq/tests directory and unzip it. Then you can
run the jquery132/test/index.html file inside there to start the tests.

The tests were changed in a couple ways. For the tests I modified,
you can look for //JRB changed: to find the original test construction.
Things that were changed:

1) acme requires spaces between CSS3 selectors, where sizzle does
not ("div>span" fails in acme, but works in sizzle). There is a
dtk.org bug on it, and it is allowed by the CSS3 spec to not have
spaces so hopefully that incompatibility can go away after a while.

2) sizzle supports some psuedos like :last, :first: :odd, :even that
work on the list of matched elements, not just individual elements or
their children. This is a more fundamental change to acme, but it is probably
doable.

3) The XML tests and ajax tests that call out to files fail because of
some weird timing interaction between the jquery unit test thing and
our XHR code. I believe since our code has a timer where we check the
status of the XHR calls instead of using load callbacks directly on
the XHR callbacks, something is confused in jquery -- the failure case
is fired before our callbacks work. If only they used deferreds. ;)
To get those tests to sort of work, I modified qunit/testrunner.js's process()
method to be like so:

function process() {
	if(config.queue.length && !config.blocking){
		setTimeout(function(){
		if(config.queue.length && !config.blocking){
			config.queue.shift()();
			process();
		}
		}, 100);
	}
}

Change 100 above to tune it depending on your patience and how much
you want to make sure the tests have enough time to run. With 100, you
can see some of the ajax tests passing.

From some previous notes (I have not checked more recently), it looks
like the compat layer fires "ajaxStop" more than jquery, I think due
to how we do our async in-flight testing, so that messes up some of
the testing in the ajax calls, but I think that is a detail that is
fine to go with. I just have to make sure that is really the cause of
a test failure and not something else. So I will probably need to
modify the tests more.


-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Installation instructions
